### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Acris, Ganimian, King, and Marple-Cantrell report a clean school-randomized trial of a USAID-funded civics program in 140 Liberian public primary schools (70 treatment, 70 control, stratified by county and district) and find that after one school year grade 3–4 students in treatment schools scored 0.379 SD (SE 0.086) higher on a civic knowledge assessment (Table 3, Panel A), with the gain concentrated in the "knowing" cognitive domain (0.370) and in the society-and-systems (0.284) and participation (0.364) content domains, and no detectable effect on reasoning-and-applying (0.076, SE 0.085), civic principles, civic identities, or three self-reported civic behaviors (index 0.003, SE 0.015; Table 6). The core estimate is credibly identified: baseline balance is good (joint F p = .444), attrition is 15% and non-differential (−0.006, SE 0.020), contamination is measured rather than assumed (6 of 70 control principals reported teaching civics), and the effect sits far from any significance threshold. The field can cite this as the first school-based experimental evidence on children's civic knowledge in a low-income, post-conflict setting, and as good feasibility evidence that individual take-home textbooks and a timetabled twice-weekly subject can be delivered with high fidelity in such a system. What needs qualification is almost everything built on top of that number. The assessment was written to the treatment curriculum and given to control students who mostly received no civics instruction at all, so 0.38 SD is the effect of teaching a subject on a test of that subject; the comparisons to LMIC math-and-reading meta-analyses ("more than double") and the conversion to "38 ICCS points" (p. 11) rest on an unstated and unsupported equivalence of standard deviations and should not travel. The intervention is a four-part bundle (textbooks, 2-day training, twice-weekly lessons, twice-monthly monitoring), so the paper's third claimed contribution — a lesson for the textbook-provision literature — and the abstract's "textbook-centered instruction" mechanism cannot be separated from added instructional time, and the classroom observations (60 schools, one lesson each, with the comparison lesson in control schools unspecified) describe what treatment classrooms did, not what caused the gains. The engagement null covers three dichotomized prosocial self-reports with control means of 0.75–0.84, while attitude outcomes — a primary outcome in the study's AEA registry entry — are reported only "upon request." The one significant heterogeneity result is understated: Table 4, column 5 implies an effect of −0.18 SD (n.s.) in non-rural districts and about +0.53 SD in rural ones, which the Discussion softens to "somewhat larger" and the Conclusion to "across a broad range of students," though the specification swaps strata for county fixed effects and the number of districts is never reported. Finally, the pre-analysis plan was first published June 24, 2024 — the intervention's listed end date and roughly nine months after baseline — and the PDF carries no data, code, or software statement, so the subscale, heterogeneity, and mechanism results should be read as exploratory and nothing beyond the arithmetic of the printed tables can be independently verified. The right posture: rely on the headline knowledge effect and the knowing-versus-reasoning profile as printed in Table 3; attach caveats to the magnitude benchmarks, the textbook mechanism, the breadth of the engagement null, and the generality of the effect across urban and rural districts; and treat "a scalable model for strengthening democratic foundations in fragile states" as aspiration rather than finding.

#### Key Strengths

- Design and execution are sound and well documented: school-level randomization matching school-wide delivery, stratification by county and district, 140 clusters, good balance on 13 baseline characteristics (Table 1, joint F = 1.011, p = .444), 85% follow-up with a −0.6 percentage-point differential and a null joint attrition test (Table 2, p = .323), measured contamination (6 of 70 control principals teaching civics, 8 of 70 with textbooks, 3 with both), and reported implementation fidelity (textbooks in 100% of treatment schools, 96% of students confirming receipt, 94% training participation, 38-minute observed lessons).
- The headline effect is large and precisely estimated (0.379 SD, SE 0.086, t ≈ 4.4; Table 3), the quantile and baseline-percentile analyses show positive point estimates throughout the distribution (Figure 1), and there is no detectable heterogeneity by gender, grade, household assets, or home language (Table 4, columns 1–4). As evidence that Liberian children learn curricular civics content when it is actually delivered, the result is solid.
- The paper reports its nulls candidly and in the tables: reasoning-and-applying, civic principles, civic identities, and all three engagement items are shown with standard errors; the abstract states the engagement null; ceiling effects on engagement and the fixed-effects substitution behind the rural estimate are flagged by the authors themselves.
- The setting is genuinely under-studied — primary-grade, school-based civics in a low-income, post-conflict African country — and the Discussion's generalizability paragraph (p. 17) is more explicit than most, naming the three features of Liberia that bound the result and candidate replication settings.
- The headline specification (Equation 1: ANCOVA with baseline score, strata fixed effects, school-clustered SEs) is stated plainly, and the reported numbers reconcile: sample flow (167 − 22 = 145 eligible; 44 + 48 + 48 = 140), Ns (1,101 + 1,006 = 2,107; 936 + 848 = 1,784), follow-up rates (936/1,101 = 0.850), Table 5 row sums, the 15-percentile and 8-percentage-point derivations, and significance stars against coefficient/SE ratios all check.

#### Key Concerns

- The estimand is narrower than the framing. Control schools mostly taught no civics (pp. 5–6) and the test was "aligned with the Grade 3 and Grade 4 Liberian civic education curriculum" that only treatment schools received (p. 8), so 0.38 SD measures instruction in a body of content against a no-instruction counterfactual on a test of that content. The benchmarks on p. 11 — "more than double" the 0.08–0.15 SD LMIC meta-analytic range and "roughly equivalent to a 38-point increase on the ICCS scale," moving "from Colombia (482) to just above the international average (517)" — treat it as a general achievement gain. The meta-analysis comparison carries a subject-matter caveat but not an alignment caveat; the ICCS conversion carries no caveat at all and assumes one SD among Liberian third and fourth graders equals 100 ICCS points among eighth graders in 24 countries. The literature reviewer also notes the "467 to 586" range omits at least two lower-scoring ICCS 2016 participants (Peru, Dominican Republic).
- The mechanism and textbook claims outrun the design. Textbooks came bundled with a new timetabled subject, teacher training, and twice-monthly NGO monitoring (pp. 6–7), so nothing separates materials from instructional time; the contrast with textbook-provision nulls (Glewwe et al., 2009; Sabarwal et al., 2014), where books were added to subjects already taught, is not like-for-like. The classroom-observation evidence (Table 5) is descriptive, from one observed lesson in each of 60 schools, with observers necessarily unblinded, the comparison lesson in control schools unspecified, and no measure of "rote memorization" despite the p. 3 claim; the Teach Primary pedagogy tool was dropped for reliability (fn. 4). The student textbook-use figures (63% vs. 2%, p. 12) appear in no exhibit in the main paper.
- The engagement null is thinner than "no impact on students' civic engagement" (abstract) suggests, and the null subscales are imprecise. Engagement is three self-reported prosocial items dichotomized from a 4-point scale with control means of 0.751–0.843 (Table 6); attitudes, which the registry lists as a primary outcome, are "available upon request" (fn. 3); and the civic identities domain — the content closest to the paper's post-conflict rationale — shows 0.021 (SE 0.067) without discussion. Realized power is below plan (footnote 1's MDE of 0.17 SD assumed a 0.40 baseline–endline correlation and 15 students per cluster; the realized SE of 0.086 implies an MDE near 0.24 SD, the baseline slope is 0.226, and the endline cluster size is about 12.7), so the "null" subscales cannot rule out effects of roughly +0.15 to +0.27 SD, and the knowing-versus-reasoning contrast is never formally tested.
- The rural heterogeneity result is understated and fragile at once. Table 4, column 5 gives a treatment coefficient of −0.177 (SE 0.219) for non-rural districts and an interaction of 0.706 (SE 0.238), implying roughly zero effect in urban districts and about 0.53 SD in rural ones; the Results call this "substantially stronger gains in rural schools relative to urban schools" (p. 12), the Discussion "somewhat larger improvements" that were "broadly shared" (p. 16), and the Conclusion gains "across a broad range of students" (p. 17), and neither the abstract nor the generalizability paragraph mentions it. At the same time the specification drops the strata fixed effects for county fixed effects (the paper's stated reason — that because rurality is district-level the strata fixed effects "cannot be included" — is not right, since only the rural main effect is absorbed and the interaction remains identified), "rural district" is undefined, and the number of districts behind the moderator is unreported.
- Pre-registration, reproducibility, and several prose–exhibit lapses limit what can be verified. The pre-analysis plan was "first published on June 24, 2024" (fn. 5), the intervention's registry end date and about nine months after baseline, and the paper neither says so nor reports which outcomes were pre-specified; the PDF has no data availability, code, or software statement; the outcome metric is described as standardized "at baseline" (p. 10) but "in the control group" in the Table 3 note (endline control mean exactly 0.000 [1.000]); "all analyses control for students' baseline assessment scores" (p. 10) does not match the Table 5 or Table 6 notes; the attrition sentence (p. 8) reports the age × treatment interaction (−0.015, significant only at 10%) as the treatment-group age gradient and calls it "statistically significant"; and fidelity statistics shift between sections ("100% of teachers," p. 2, vs. "100% of treatment schools," p. 7; "96% … confirming receipt," p. 7, vs. "96% … receiving and regularly using," p. 17) with no exhibit for any of them.

#### What to Rely On

- After one school year, the program raised scores on a curriculum-aligned civic knowledge assessment by 0.379 SD (SE 0.086; 95% CI ≈ 0.21–0.55; Table 3, Panel A). This is the load-bearing, well-identified result; quote it as the effect of introducing a structured civics course, in the paper's endline-control-SD units.
- The profile of the gain: large on the "knowing" domain (0.370, SE 0.078) and on society-and-systems (0.284) and participation (0.364) content, small and insignificant on reasoning-and-applying (0.076), principles (0.091), and identities (0.021) (Table 3, Panels B–C) — as a description of point estimates, not as a tested contrast.
- Point-estimate gains at every percentile of the endline distribution and at every baseline-score percentile (Figure 1), with somewhat larger gains in the middle, and no detectable heterogeneity by gender, grade, household assets, or home language (Table 4, columns 1–4).
- Feasibility and fidelity: textbooks and a timetabled twice-weekly subject were delivered at scale in a low-resource system; treatment teachers taught with a textbook 57% of class time versus 15% in control and used the blackboard 25% versus 50% (Table 5, Panel B); time on learning activities was unchanged at about 77% (Panel A); whole-class engagement rose from 71% to 87% of class time (Panel C).
- A precisely estimated one-year null on three self-reported everyday behaviors — helping classmates, helping neighbors, obeying community laws — with the index CI about −0.03 to +0.03 and no item upper bound above roughly 8 percentage points (Table 6). Describe these as prosocial self-reports near ceiling, not civic or political engagement generally.
- Low, balanced attrition (85% follow-up; treatment differential −0.006, SE 0.020; joint interaction test p = .323; Table 2) and good baseline balance (Table 1).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "More than double" the LMIC meta-analytic average and "a 38-point increase on the ICCS scale" (p. 11) — the test was aligned to a curriculum the control group did not receive, the SD-equivalence with the ICCS scale is assumed rather than shown, and the quoted ICCS floor of 467 omits lower-scoring participants; do not carry these into citations or briefs.
- "Knowledge gains were driven by textbook-centered instruction rather than shifts in pedagogy" (pp. 2–3) and the contribution to the textbook-provision literature (pp. 3, 16–17) — a four-component bundle cannot isolate textbooks; the observation data are descriptive, unblinded, and lack a specified comparison lesson; and the 63% vs. 2% student textbook-use figures have no exhibit.
- "The program had no impact on students' civic engagement" (abstract) — three dichotomized self-report items with control means of 0.75–0.84; attitudes (a registered primary outcome) are unreported; read as "no detectable change in three everyday prosocial self-reports within one year."
- "Positive effects across the achievement distribution" (abstract), "broadly shared" (p. 16), and "across a diverse student body" (p. 17) — the Figure 1 confidence bands include zero at roughly the top fifth of the endline distribution, and the point estimates in Table 4, column 5 imply no gain in urban districts.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The top-fifth observation does not contradict the abstract. The point estimates are positive across the whole distribution, the lower band crosses zero only above about the 84th percentile, and p. 12 discloses the loss of significance; that is compression at the top, not a contradiction. The second half of this bullet stands: Table 4, column 5 implies about −0.18 SD (not significant) in non-rural districts and about +0.53 SD in rural ones, so "broadly shared" (p. 16) and "across a broad range of students" (p. 17) fail. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered figure and table, and held after a blind second reading.

- The rural interaction itself (0.706, Table 4, column 5) — estimated with county rather than strata fixed effects, on an undefined "rural district" indicator with an unreported number of districts; do not cite the rural concentration as established, but do not cite the pooled effect as uniform across settings either.
- "Gains concentrated in factual knowledge" as a contrast — the subscale CIs reach about +0.24 SD (reasoning) and +0.27 SD (principles), the percent-correct subscales have unreported item counts and reliability, and the difference between domains is never tested.
- "The first experimental evidence on the effectiveness of civic education in a low-income, post-conflict setting" (Conclusion, p. 17) — defensible only with the introduction's qualifiers ("school-based," "student civic outcomes"); the literature reviewer identifies randomized adult civic-education trials in Liberia (Mvukiyehe & Samii, 2017) and Mali (Gottlieb, 2016) that are not cited.
- Several characterizations of prior work — Green et al. (2011), Morduchowicz et al. (1996), and NORC (2019) as high-income-country studies (p. 16; Argentina and Georgia are middle-income); Morduchowicz et al. as a secondary-level evaluation (p. 3); Nie & Hillygus (2001) and Niemi & Junn (1998) as longitudinal evidence on childhood civic knowledge (p. 3); Alan et al. (2021) and Dhar et al. (2022) as examples of complements "harder to implement in low-resource settings" (p. 16) when both changed behavior through school-delivered curricula in middle-income public schools. Verify before repeating.
- Any number quoted from the prose without an exhibit — student textbook use (63%/2%), every fidelity statistic (100%, 96%, 94%, 94%, 38 minutes, 29 of 48), "baseline levels of reported civic engagement were already high" (p. 16; Table 6 shows only endline means), and the attrition gradient ("1.5 percentage points for each year of age," p. 8, which is the interaction coefficient, significant at 10%, not the within-treatment gradient of about 2.3 points).
- "A scalable model for strengthening democratic foundations in fragile states" (p. 17) — no cost data are reported, delivery ran through donor-funded NGOs with twice-monthly monitoring the authors concede may be hard to sustain, and none of the outcomes tied to democratic foundations (identities, attitudes, behaviors) moved.
- The study's status as pre-registered and its verifiability — registration was first published June 24, 2024, after baseline and at the listed end of the intervention; no PAP-deviation discussion, data, code, or software statement exists in the PDF; the outcome standardization is described two different ways; and thirteen supplementary items (Figures A.1–A.2, Table A.1, Appendices B.1–B.5) that carry instrument details, item counts, and the theory of change do not travel with the article.

#### Verification notes

- Headline and subscale effects (abstract, pp. 2, 11 vs. Table 3): 0.38/0.379***, 0.37/0.370***, 0.36/0.364***, 0.28/0.284***; nulls 0.091, 0.021, 0.076 unstarred — CONFIRMED (rendered p. 11).
- Rural specification (Table 4, column 5): treatment −0.177 (0.219), covariate −0.335 (0.214), interaction 0.706*** (0.238); implied rural effect ≈ 0.53, urban ≈ −0.18 — CONFIRMED (rendered p. 14).
- Student textbook use "63% vs. 2%" (p. 12) has no row in Table 5, whose Panel B is labeled "(teachers)" — CONFIRMED (rendered p. 15).
- Attrition sentence (p. 8) vs. Table 2, Panel B: Age −0.008 (0.006), Age × Treatment −0.015* (0.008); the 1.5-point figure is the interaction and is significant at 10% only — CONFIRMED (rendered p. 9).
- Standardization: "at baseline" (p. 10) vs. "in the control group" (Table 3 note) with endline control at 0.000 [1.000] and baseline treatment at 0.043 [1.075] (Table 1) — CONFIRMED.
- Figure 1: the lower 95% band crosses zero at roughly the top fifth of the endline distribution (Panel A) and near the top of the baseline distribution (Panel B) — CONFIRMED (rendered p. 13).
- Table 5 row sums to 1.00 within each panel; significance stars consistent with coefficient/SE ratios in Tables 2–6 — CONFIRMED.
- Fidelity text shifts ("100% of teachers," p. 2 vs. "100% of treatment schools," p. 7; "confirming receipt," p. 7 vs. "receiving and regularly using," p. 17) — CONFIRMED from the text.
- Power arithmetic: 2.8 × 0.086 ≈ 0.24 SD realized MDE vs. 0.17 planned (fn. 1); baseline slope 0.226 (Table 4, column 6); endline cluster size 1,784/140 ≈ 12.7 — CONFIRMED.
- Implied grade effects from Table 4, column 1 (0.431 grade 3; 0.431 − 0.105 = 0.326 grade 4) — CONFIRMED.
- Conclusion (p. 17) drops the introduction's "student civic outcomes" qualifier from the first-evidence claim — CONFIRMED.
- AEA RCT Registry AEARCTR-0013817 (fetched independently): initial registration June 14, 2024; first published June 24, 2024; intervention September 25, 2023 to June 24, 2024; primary outcomes "student civic knowledge, student civic attitudes, student civic behaviors"; no public PAP document — CONFIRMED.
- Reproducibility review's registry discrepancy on stratification ("by county" vs. the paper's county and district) — CORRECTED: the registry line describes the 44/48/48 sample allocation across counties, not necessarily the randomization strata; not a clear discrepancy.
- Reproducibility review's statement that the registry lists grades 3–4 (vs. the paper's grades 1–6) as receiving the intervention — COULD NOT CHECK (not returned by the overseer's fetch).
- Literature review's external claims (Mvukiyehe & Samii 2017 and Gottlieb 2016 as uncited adult civic-education RCTs; ICCS 2016 scores for Peru and the Dominican Republic below 467; Morduchowicz et al. 1996 as a grade 5–6 program; McEwan 2015 category means) — COULD NOT CHECK against the paper; consistent with the overseer's own knowledge but not independently verified here.
- Absence of any data availability, code, or software statement in the PDF — CONFIRMED by text search ("upon request" appears only in footnotes 3–4; "replication" only in the Discussion's replication-studies sentence).

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This is a clean school-level cluster RCT (140 schools, stratified by district). It has good baseline balance, low and non-differential attrition, and a standard estimator (ANCOVA with strata fixed effects and school-clustered SEs). The headline intent-to-treat effect on civic knowledge (0.379 SD, SE 0.086; p. 11, Table 3, Panel A) is credibly identified. Several claims built around that estimate are less secure: how large the effect is, what drove it, the null on engagement, and the rural heterogeneity. They depend on a curriculum-aligned researcher test, a bundled treatment, a thin self-report engagement measure, descriptive observation data, and one specification that drops the strata fixed effects. The pre-analysis plan was registered after baseline data collection, and the paper does not report which outcomes it named as primary. Readers therefore cannot treat the analysis as confirmatory.

**Strengths:**

- The school-level randomization matches the school-wide delivery of the program, which went to all of grades 1-6 in treatment schools (p. 5). Stratification by county and district (p. 5) and 140 clusters give conventional cluster-robust inference a comfortable number of clusters. [checkable]
- Baseline balance is good. None of the 13 characteristics differs significantly, the joint F-test gives p = .444, and the baseline IRT gap is 0.029 SD (SE 0.071) (p. 6, Table 1). [checkable]
- Attrition is low and balanced. 1,784 of 2,107 baseline students were reassessed (84.7%): control 936/1,101 = 85.0% and treatment 848/1,006 = 84.3%. That matches the −0.006 (0.020) differential (p. 9, Table 2, Panel A). The joint test of treatment × baseline-characteristic interactions gives p = .323 (Table 2, Panel B). [checkable]
- The estimator is appropriate and plainly specified: ANCOVA with the baseline outcome, strata fixed effects, and school-clustered SEs (p. 10, Eq. 1). The main knowledge effects are far from any significance threshold (t ≈ 4.4 overall; ≈ 4.1-5.9 for the society/systems, participation, and knowing subscales; p. 11, Table 3). They would survive any reasonable multiple-testing correction. [checkable]
- Contamination is measured, not assumed. 6 of 70 control principals reported teaching civics, 8 of 70 had the new textbooks, and 3 had both (pp. 5-6). If anything, this biases the estimates toward zero. [checkable]
- Implementation fidelity is documented. Textbooks reached all treatment schools, 96% of students reported receipt, 94% of teachers attended training, and observed lessons averaged 38 minutes (p. 7). This supports reading the ITT as close to the effect of the program as delivered. [checkable]
- Reporting is candid about nulls: the principles, identities, and reasoning subscales and all engagement items (Tables 3 and 6). The paper also flags that the rural estimate uses a different specification (pp. 12, 16). [checkable]

**Weaknesses:**

- **Registration came after baseline, and some collected outcomes go unreported.** The AEA registry entry was "first published on June 24, 2024" (p. 18, fn. 5). Baseline data were collected at the start of the 2023-24 school year, and endline "near the end of that same school year" (p. 8). So registration clearly post-dates baseline. The paper gives no endline field dates, so it cannot be confirmed whether registration also came during or after endline collection. [checkable] Student attitude measures were collected but results are "available upon request" (fn. 3). A second observation tool (Teach Primary) was piloted and excluded for "reliability concerns" (fn. 4). The paper never says which outcomes the plan named as primary, or whether there were deviations. [checkable] Readers should treat the subscale, observation, and heterogeneity results as exploratory. [judgment]
- **The size of the effect depends on how the test was built, and the benchmark comparisons overstate it.** The assessment is researcher-designed and "aligned with the Grade 3 and Grade 4 Liberian civic education curriculum" (p. 8). Control schools did not receive that curriculum (p. 5). [checkable] So part of the 0.38 SD is the effect of being taught material the control group was never exposed to. Comparing it with math and language meta-analysis averages of 0.08-0.15 SD (p. 11) is therefore not like-for-like; the authors do add a caveat. [judgment] The conversion to "a 38-point increase on the ICCS scale" (p. 11) assumes that one SD in this sample of Liberian grade 3-4 children equals one SD (100 points) on an international lower-secondary scale. Nothing supports that assumption, and readers should set this translation aside. [judgment] Two percentile translations are arithmetically correct but inherit the same problem: Φ(0.38) ≈ 0.648, the "15 percentile points" on p. 11, and 482 + 38 = 520, "just above" 517. [checkable]
- **The study had less power than planned, so the "null" subscales are imprecise.** Footnote 1 assumes a cluster size of 15, a baseline-endline correlation of 0.40, and an MDE of 0.17 SD (p. 18). The realized endline cluster size is 1,784/140 ≈ 12.7. The ANCOVA slope on standardized baseline IRT is 0.226 (0.034) (p. 14, Table 4, col. 6), which points to a baseline-endline correlation well below 0.40. The realized SE of 0.086 implies an MDE of about 2.8 × 0.086 ≈ 0.24 SD. [checkable] The 95% CIs on the "null" subscales run to about +0.27 SD (principles: 0.091 ± 1.96 × 0.090), +0.24 SD (reasoning: 0.076 ± 1.96 × 0.085), and +0.15 SD (identities) (p. 11, Table 3). [checkable] "Primarily factual knowledge" is a reasonable description of the point estimates. It is not an established contrast: the knowing-vs-reasoning difference is never tested formally, and the percent-correct subscales have unknown and possibly unequal reliability (p. 10). [judgment]
- **The mechanism claims go beyond what the design can show.** The treatment bundles several things: a new subject with twice-weekly dedicated lessons, textbooks, 2-day training, and twice-monthly implementer monitoring (p. 6). Nothing in the design separates their effects. [checkable] Claims that the gains were "driven by textbook-centered instruction rather than shifts in pedagogy" (p. 2), and comparisons to textbook-only trials (Glewwe et al., Sabarwal et al.; p. 17), treat the program as a textbook intervention. Those trials added books to subjects already being taught. Here, the difference is closer to civics instruction versus little or none. [judgment]
- **The classroom observation evidence is thin and its comparison group is unclear.** The data cover 60 schools, one row per school, with nine Stallings snapshots per lesson (p. 10; p. 15, Table 5). The paper does not say which subject or lesson was observed in control classrooms, where the new civics course did not exist. [checkable] Observers could not have been blind to treatment, since textbook use is the outcome. [judgment] The text reports student textbook use of 63% vs. 2% of class time (p. 12), but Table 5 has no row for student materials use. That figure cannot be checked against any table in the main text. [checkable]
- **The engagement null is weaker evidence than its framing suggests.** Engagement is three self-reported items, dichotomized from a 4-point scale (p. 10; p. 15, Table 6 note). Control means are already 0.751-0.843 (Table 6). [checkable] The CI arithmetic is right: 0.036 + 1.96 × 0.023 ≈ 0.081, which supports "rule out … approximately 8 percentage points" (p. 12). The index CI is roughly −0.03 to +0.03 (0.003 ± 1.96 × 0.015). [checkable] Still, this is a narrow and ceiling-prone measure of prosocial self-reports. It should be read as "no detectable change in three self-reported everyday behaviors." It should not be read as the broad claim that the program "had no impact on students' civic engagement" (abstract). [judgment]
- **The rural heterogeneity result is fragile and understated.** The paper says strata fixed effects "cannot be included" because rurality is district-level (p. 12). Only the rural main effect is absorbed by district strata; the treatment × rural interaction would still be identified with strata fixed effects. [judgment; standard econometrics] In the county-FE specification, the treatment coefficient for urban districts is −0.177 (0.219), against an implied rural effect of 0.529 (p. 14, Table 4, col. 5). [checkable] So the point estimates imply no gain in urban districts. The discussion calls this only "somewhat larger improvements … in rural schools" (p. 16). [judgment] The number of districts, which is the effective sample for this moderator, is not reported in the main text. [checkable]
- **There are small inconsistencies between the text and the tables.** The text says IRT scores are "standardized to have mean zero and SD one at baseline" (p. 10). The Table 3 note says scores are standardized "in the control group," and the endline control mean is 0.000 [1.000] (p. 11). So endline effects are in endline-control-SD units. [checkable] The age × treatment attrition interaction is called "statistically significant" (p. 8) but is significant only at 10%: −0.015 (0.008) (p. 9, Table 2, Panel B). [checkable] Neither affects the conclusions.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Rely on the overall ITT on the researcher-built civic knowledge test (0.379 SD, 95% CI ≈ 0.21-0.55; p. 11, Table 3, Panel A). It is the load-bearing, well-identified result. Read it as the effect of introducing a curriculum-aligned civics course, not as a generic learning gain comparable to LMIC math and reading benchmarks.
- Do not carry forward the ICCS "38-point" translation (p. 11) into citations or policy briefs. The two populations and scales are not commensurable.
- Treat "gains concentrated in factual knowledge" as a description of point estimates. Nulls on principles, identities, and reasoning cannot rule out effects of about 0.15-0.27 SD (Table 3).
- Treat the engagement result as a null on three ceiling-prone self-reports (Table 6), not evidence that civics instruction cannot change children's civic behavior. The unreported attitude outcomes (fn. 3) leave the attitudes channel unexamined.
- Do not cite the rural interaction (Table 4, col. 5) as a finding. If you use it, note that it implies roughly zero effect in urban districts, comes from a specification that departs from the main model by dropping strata FE, and rests on an unreported number of districts.
- Read the classroom-observation results (Table 5) as descriptive confirmation that treatment classrooms used the new textbooks. They do not show that textbook-centered pedagogy caused the gains. The comparison lessons in control schools are unspecified.
- Before building on subscale or heterogeneity results, check the AEA registry entry (AEARCTR-0013817) against the reported outcomes, keeping in mind it was published after baseline. Also check the Supplemental Appendix, which this review could not access, for item counts, reliabilities, and analytic-sample balance.
- For policy extrapolation, note that the counterfactual is essentially no civics course. The paper does not show whether the twice-weekly lessons displaced time from other subjects, and it offers no cost data.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Design and identification.* The experimental core is sound. Randomization is at the school level, which matches the program's school-wide delivery to grades 1-6 and limits within-school spillovers (p. 5). Stratification by county and district with 70/70 allocation gives 140 clusters. Balance on 13 baseline characteristics is good (p. 6, Table 1: joint F = 1.011, p = .444), and the "Difference" column correctly includes strata fixed effects. [checkable] The sampling arithmetic is internally consistent: 167 − 16 − 4 − 2 = 145 eligible, and 44 + 48 + 48 = 140 selected (p. 5). [checkable] Treatment schools contributed fewer baseline students than control schools (1,006 vs. 1,101, or about 14.4 vs. 15.7 per school; Table 1). The paper does not say whether randomization or assignment was known before students were selected at baseline. Student selection depended on attendance and on enumerator top-ups across grades (p. 8). The good baseline balance makes this a minor concern, but it is an unreported design detail. [checkable: timing not stated; judgment: low consequence] The effective sample is also selected. The target was 2,800 students; 2,107 were assessed because of low enrollment and attendance (pp. 5, 8). So the estimates describe students present on assessment days, not all enrolled children. [checkable]

*Attrition.* Follow-up is 85% with a differential of −0.6 percentage points (p. 9, Table 2, Panel A). The joint interaction test is null (Panel B, p = .323). By conventional standards such as the WWC attrition boundaries, this is a low-attrition trial. [checkable for the numbers; judgment for the standard] The age × treatment interaction (−0.015, p < .10) is small. The treatment main effect in Panel B (0.183) is evaluated at age zero and has no substantive meaning. [checkable] Balance on the analytic sample and bounds such as Lee bounds are not shown in the main text. Given how small the differential is, their absence is unlikely to matter. [judgment]

*Estimation.* Equation 1 is a standard ANCOVA with strata fixed effects and school-clustered SEs (p. 10). This is the right default, and 140 clusters is ample for asymptotic cluster-robust inference. [judgment] I checked significance stars against coefficient/SE ratios across Tables 2-6 and found them internally consistent; for example, 0.146/0.055 ≈ 2.65 is marked ** (Table 5), and −0.034/0.021 ≈ 1.62 is unstarred (Table 6). [checkable] Row proportions in each panel of Table 5 sum to 1.00 within rounding. [checkable] One diagnostic is worth noting. The coefficient on standardized baseline IRT is only 0.226 (Table 4, col. 6), where power calculations assumed a baseline-endline correlation of 0.40 (fn. 1). The baseline test appears to carry limited signal about endline knowledge. That is plausible for young children tested on content most had not yet studied, but it has two consequences. Precision is lower than designed (realized MDE ≈ 0.24 vs. 0.17 SD). And the "effects by baseline score" analyses (Figure 1, Panel B; Table 4, col. 6) condition on a noisy proxy for prior knowledge, which flattens any true gradient. [checkable for the numbers; judgment for the interpretation]

*Measurement of knowledge.* The assessment borrows the ICCS content and cognitive framework and uses a pooled 2PL IRT model linked through common items (pp. 8-10). That is a credible approach to scaling. The main text does not report item counts, the number of anchor items, reliability, or whether grade 3 and grade 4 students took the same form. These details were said to be in the Supplemental Appendix, which could not be checked. [checkable: absent from main text] The subscales use standardized percent-correct because "there are not enough items per domain to estimate separate IRT models" (p. 10). Their reliability is therefore probably modest and may differ across domains. That matters for the knowing-vs-reasoning contrast, because a less reliable subscale mechanically yields a smaller standardized effect. [judgment] The more important interpretive issue is alignment. The test was built to the new curriculum and given to control children who never received it. That is the right test for asking whether the program taught its content. It is the wrong basis for comparing magnitudes with general-achievement meta-analyses, or for mapping onto the ICCS reporting scale. [judgment] One more procedural gap: enumerators assisted students with the written assessment (p. 5), and the paper does not say whether enumerators were blind to treatment status. [checkable: not stated]

*Distributional results.* Figure 1, Panel A (p. 13) shows positive point estimates for the quantile treatment effects across the distribution. The 95% band clearly includes zero above roughly the 80th-85th percentile. The text's "first-order stochastically dominates" and "outperformed … at every percentile" (p. 12) describe point estimates, not a formal dominance test. [checkable from the figure; judgment on wording] Panel A is also unconditional: no strata or baseline adjustment is described in the note. Its mid-distribution effects of about 0.5 are therefore not directly comparable to the 0.379 ANCOVA estimate. [checkable from the note] Convergence at the top could reflect a test ceiling as much as smaller learning gains. [judgment]

*Heterogeneity.* Only the rural interaction is significant (0.706, SE 0.238; Table 4, col. 5). Three features make it fragile. First, the authors drop the strata fixed effects, saying they "cannot be included" (p. 12). That is incorrect. District strata absorb the rural main effect but not the treatment × rural interaction, so the preferred specification was available. [judgment; standard econometrics] Second, the moderator varies only at the district level, and the number of districts is not reported. The effective comparison may rest on a handful of districts, and school-level clustering may understate uncertainty about a district-level moderator. [checkable: count not reported; judgment on inference] Third, the implied urban-district effect is −0.177 (SE 0.219). The discussion frames the result as "somewhat larger improvements … in rural schools" (p. 16), but the point estimates actually imply the program did nothing in urban districts. That would matter a great deal for scale-up if it held. [checkable for the coefficient; judgment for its implications] The grade estimates are also worth a look. The implied grade 3 effect is 0.431 and the grade 4 effect about 0.326 (Table 4, col. 1). Meanwhile the significant domains (society and systems, participation) track grade 4 textbook content (p. 7), while identities, which is closest to grade 3 content, shows 0.021. Without domain-by-grade results, readers cannot tell whether the test was equally aligned to both grades' curricula. [judgment]

*Instructional practices.* The observation study was run in a random 30/30 subset of schools, with one school-level row each (p. 15, Table 5). It convincingly shows that treatment teachers used the new textbooks (0.402, SE 0.080) and used the blackboard less. [checkable] Its role in the causal story is weaker. The paper does not state what was observed in control classrooms, where no civics course existed, so the comparison may be civics-with-textbooks against some other subject. [checkable: not stated] Nine snapshots of what appears to be a single lesson per school give noisy classroom measures. Observers necessarily knew treatment status. The whole-class engagement effect (0.146, p < .05) is also accompanied by a large treatment-arm SD in "no students engaged" (0.037 [0.183]), which suggests influential outlier classrooms. [checkable for the numbers; judgment for the interpretation] The 63% vs. 2% student textbook-use figures (p. 12) do not appear in any main-text table. [checkable] These data describe what changed in classrooms. They cannot show that textbook-centered instruction, rather than dedicated civics time, training, or monitoring, produced the knowledge gains. [judgment]

*Engagement.* The null is precisely estimated for what it measures. The index effect is 0.003 (SE 0.015), and the upper CI for "obey laws" is about 8 points (p. 15, Table 6). [checkable] But it measures three self-reported behaviors, dichotomized, with control means of 75-84%. The authors themselves raise the ceiling issue (p. 16). Social-desirability or demand effects would, if anything, push treatment-arm reports upward, so the null is not easily explained away by reporting bias. [judgment] Still, three prosocial items are thin grounds for the broader conclusion that textbook-centered civics "had no impact on students' civic engagement" (abstract) or that content delivery "is unlikely to shift behavior in this age group" (p. 16). The unreported attitude outcomes (fn. 3) would have been the natural intermediate test. [checkable for fn. 3; judgment for the rest]

*Registration and analytic flexibility.* The registry entry was first published on June 24, 2024 (fn. 5). Baseline was collected at the start of the 2023-24 school year, and endline near its end (p. 8). [checkable] The main text does not say what the plan specified, whether the domain and cognitive subscales, observation outcomes, and heterogeneity dimensions were pre-specified, or whether there were deviations. [checkable: not stated] Footnote 1 describes the power calculation as "ex ante," yet its assumed cluster size of 15 matches the realized baseline average exactly (p. 8). That is consistent with the calculation having been updated after baseline, though it proves nothing. [checkable for the match; judgment for the inference] The headline result is too strong to be a product of specification search. The main risk from post-baseline registration and unreported outcomes applies to the secondary claims: which subscales "worked," the engagement framing, and heterogeneity.

*Bottom line.* The design firmly supports the claim that introducing this civics program raised children's performance on a curriculum-aligned civic knowledge test by a large, precisely estimated amount within one school year. It does not firmly support four further claims: that the gain is large by general LMIC-education standards, that textbooks specifically (rather than the bundle) drove it, that the program has no effect on civic behavior broadly, or that effects are concentrated in rural areas. I rate the methods Adequate rather than Strong because much of the paper's interpretive and policy framing rests on these weaker layers, not because the core experiment is flawed. My confidence is moderate because the Supplemental Appendix and the pre-analysis plan's contents could not be examined.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper cites a broad and mostly relevant set of sources on civic education, political socialization, Liberian context, and LMIC schooling. It is honest that its effect-size benchmarks are imperfect (p. 11) and that the findings come from one country (p. 17). But its positioning is weaker than its reference list suggests. The headline novelty claim ("first experimental evaluation... in a low-income, post-conflict context," pp. 2, 17) holds only in a narrow form. Several antecedents are placed in the wrong category: Argentina and Georgia are called high-income contexts, and a 5th/6th-grade Argentine study is counted as secondary-level. The paper frames its textbook contribution against textbook-only provision studies. It does not engage the structured-pedagogy literature, which is the closest match to the actual intervention bundle, or experimental work on education and civic outcomes in Liberia and sub-Saharan Africa. Readers should treat the paper as a credible single RCT that confirms a familiar pattern: knowledge moves, behavior does not. It does not overturn prior understanding of what civic education requires.

**Strengths:**

- The civic-education citations span political science (Finkel & Ernst, 2005; Green et al., 2011; Campbell, 2008, 2019), education (Kahne & Sporte, 2008; Torney-Purta et al., 2001; Niemi & Junn, 1998), the IEA/ICCS tradition (Schulz et al., 2016, 2018), systematic reviews (Manning & Edwards, 2014; Donbavand & Hoskins, 2021), and developmental psychology on peer influence (Brechwald & Prinstein, 2011; Laursen & Veenstra, 2021). [checkable: text pp. 2-3, 7, 16; references pp. 18-22]
- The paper states a real theoretical tension, knowledge-first versus participatory civic pedagogy, and frames the study as evidence on the knowledge side (text, p. 2). This gives readers a clear way to place the result. [checkable]
- It is candid about benchmark limits. It warns that the LMIC meta-analyses it compares against cover math and language, not civics (text, p. 11). It also says the 0.38 SD knowledge gain (Table 3, p. 11) should be read with caution against those benchmarks. [checkable]
- The two textbook-provision studies it contrasts with are characterized accurately in substance. In Glewwe, Kremer & Moulin (2009), textbooks benefited only initially high-scoring students, plausibly because of English-language difficulty. In Sabarwal, Evans & Marshak (2014), books were stored rather than distributed (text, pp. 3, 17). [checkable against the reference list; external knowledge, high confidence on substance]
- The null engagement result (Table 6, p. 15) is set against a literature that expects weak behavioral effects (text, pp. 3, 7, 16) rather than presented as a surprise, and the ceiling problem is acknowledged (text, p. 16). [checkable]

**Weaknesses:**

- **The novelty claim holds only in a narrow form.** "First experimental evaluation of a civic education program's effects on student civic outcomes in a low-income, post-conflict context" (text, p. 2; repeated p. 17) is defensible only with every qualifier in place: school-based, student outcomes, low-income, post-conflict. Randomized civic-education evaluations already exist in low-income and post-conflict settings with adults, including in Liberia itself: Mvukiyehe & Samii (2017, *World Development*) randomized NGO civic-education workshops before Liberia's 2011 election and found effects on participation-related outcomes. Gottlieb (2016, *AJPS*) randomized a civics course across 95 Malian localities. None of these is cited. [external knowledge; both confirmed by WebSearch]
- **The primary-level antecedent set is miscounted.** The paper says the "only known RCT" at the primary level is Mahéo (2018) in Canada, and it lists Morduchowicz et al. (1996) among secondary-level evaluations (text, p. 3). By published descriptions, the Argentine newspaper-in-schools program targeted 5th-6th (or 6th-7th) graders, which is primary school in Argentina's system at the time. It is unclear from what I could check whether that study was randomized. Separately, the Mahéo (2018) reference is an incomplete grey-literature entry with no publisher or URL (p. 20), so readers cannot easily verify the paper's only primary-level RCT anchor. [checkable for the reference; external knowledge plus WebSearch for Morduchowicz grade level; moderate certainty on randomization status]
- **Antecedents are mislabeled by income level, and the paper contradicts itself.** The Discussion says Green et al. (2011), Morduchowicz et al. (1996), and NORC (2019) were "implemented in HICs" (text, p. 16; similar p. 2). Argentina in the 1990s and Georgia in 2019 were middle-income countries, not high-income. The contrast "HIC participatory programs vs. LMIC textbook program" therefore rests partly on a miscategorization. [external knowledge, high confidence on World Bank classifications] There is also an internal inconsistency. On p. 7 the paper states that "lecture-based civic curricula most consistently improve factual knowledge." On p. 16 it presents the knowledge gain from textbook-centered instruction as expanding "our understanding of what forms of civic education can be effective." [checkable]
- **The closest RCT antecedent shows the same pattern, but the paper does not say so.** Green et al. (2011), as its title signals, found gains in knowledge of constitutional principles with little movement in support for civil liberties. That is the same knowledge-without-downstream-change split this paper finds. The paper instead cites Green et al. as an example of participatory HIC programs (text, pp. 2, 16). [external knowledge, fairly high confidence]
- **The textbook contribution is framed against the wrong comparison set.** The intervention combined new aligned textbooks, 2-day training, timetabled twice-weekly lessons, and twice-monthly monitoring and feedback visits (text, p. 6-7). That is a structured-pedagogy package, not textbook provision. The paper contrasts it only with textbook-only provision (Glewwe et al., 2009; Sabarwal et al., 2014; text pp. 3, 17). It does not engage the structured-pedagogy evidence base: the 3ie review by Snilstveit et al. (2016); Piper and colleagues' Kenya PRIMR/Tusome work and RTI's work on teachers' guides; and Liberia's own EGRA Plus trial (Piper & Korda, 2010). The paper cites the "Smart Buys" report (Akyeampong et al., 2023) only for rote pedagogy (text, p. 2), yet that report rates structured pedagogy as a top buy. It also omits the most relevant Liberian school RCT, Romero, Sandefur & Sandholtz (2020, *AER*), on Partnership Schools for Liberia. The claim of "new insight into how instructional materials can support learning" (text, p. 3) is therefore oversold. [external knowledge, high confidence that these studies exist; judgment on relevance]
- **Earlier positive textbook evidence is omitted.** "Prior studies have found limited average effects of textbook provision" (text, p. 3) rests on two studies. It omits earlier positive textbook-provision evidence, such as Heyneman, Jamison & Montenegro (1984, published in *EEPA*), on the Philippines. [external knowledge, moderate confidence on the exact citation]
- **The effect-size benchmarks are underqualified.** The comparison to "average effects of between 0.08 and 0.15 SDs" (Evans & Yuan, 2022; McEwan, 2015; text, p. 11) omits two known sources of inflation. First, the assessment was built to align with the treatment textbooks (text, p. 8). The methods literature shows that researcher-designed, treatment-aligned tests yield substantially larger effects (Cheung & Slavin, 2016; Kraft, 2020), and neither is cited. Second, the control group received essentially no civics instruction (text, pp. 5-6). My recollection is also that McEwan's 0.15 is the largest *category* mean (computers/technology), not an upper bound on average effects, and that his instructional-materials category was nearer 0.08. [checkable for p. 8 and p. 11; external knowledge, moderate confidence on McEwan's category values]
- **The ICCS benchmark omits two participants.** The paper says the ICCS 2016 "global range" of scores ran from 467 to 586 (text, p. 11). Per the ICCS 2016 international results, Peru (438) and the Dominican Republic (381) scored below 467, so the floor is overstated. ICCS also assesses 8th graders, not grades 3-4, and the paper does not flag this when converting 0.38 SD into "38 ICCS points." [checkable for the paper's statement; external knowledge confirmed via WebSearch summary of ICCS 2016 results, moderate-high confidence]
- **The paper cites Holbein & Hillygus without engaging their argument.** The paper says childhood civic-knowledge gains "remain consequential" given longitudinal evidence (Beck & Jennings, 1982; Nie & Hillygus, 2001; Niemi & Junn, 1998; text, p. 3). Nie & Hillygus concerns what happens "in pursuit of the baccalaureate" (per its title in the reference list, p. 20), and Niemi & Junn is, to my knowledge, a cross-sectional analysis of NAEP civics data. Neither is longitudinal evidence about childhood knowledge. Holbein & Hillygus (2020) is cited only as a source of outcome categories (text, p. 7), yet the book's central argument is that civic knowledge is *not* the binding constraint on youth participation. [checkable for the titles and citation use; external knowledge, high confidence on H&H's thesis, moderate-high on Niemi & Junn's design]
- **Alan et al. and Dhar et al. show behavior change is possible in LMIC public schools.** The paper cites Alan et al. (2021) and Dhar et al. (2022) as "pedagogical complements that are harder to implement in low-resource settings" (text, p. 16). Both are randomized, school-delivered, discussion-based curricula in public schools in middle-income countries (Turkish elementary schools; government schools in Haryana, India). Both changed behaviors and attitudes. They are closer to counterexamples to the paper's pessimism about behavior than support for it. [checkable for how they are cited; external knowledge, high confidence]
- **Major adjacent literatures are missing.** The paper does not engage the political-economy and political-science literature on schooling and civic/political outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa and LMICs, or the adult civic-education evidence. Much of this work finds that education and civic curricula *do* shift attitudes and participation, sometimes in regime-dependent ways. Examples include Friedman et al. (2016) on a Kenyan scholarship RCT and deference to authority; Larreguy & Marshall (2017) on Nigeria; Croke et al. (2016) on Zimbabwe; Cantoni et al. (2017) on curriculum and ideology in China; and Finkel (2002) and Finkel, Horowitz & Rojo-Mendoza (2012) on adult civic education. The qualitative and comparative "education and conflict" tradition is also nearly absent (e.g., Bush & Saltarelli, 2000; Quaynor's review of citizenship education in post-conflict contexts, 2012), despite the paper's post-conflict framing. [external knowledge, high confidence for most; moderate for the Quaynor review]

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Cite this paper narrowly.** Cite it as a well-implemented school RCT showing that a structured, textbook-centered civics package raised curriculum-aligned civic knowledge by about 0.38 SD among Liberian grade 3-4 students (Table 3, p. 11), with no measurable effect on three self-reported behaviors (Table 6, p. 15). Do not cite it as the first civic-education RCT in a post-conflict low-income country without the "student outcomes, school-based" qualifiers: Mvukiyehe & Samii (2017) ran one in Liberia with adults.
- **Read the knowledge-without-behavior result as confirmation, not discovery.** Companion reading: Green et al. (2011) for the same split in a US RCT; Manning & Edwards (2014) and Donbavand & Hoskins (2021) for the review-level picture; Holbein & Hillygus (2020) for why knowledge gains may not translate into participation.
- **Compare it with structured-pedagogy trials, not textbook-drop studies.** Glewwe et al. (2009) and Sabarwal et al. (2014) are not the right benchmarks. Better comparisons are the structured-pedagogy literature (Snilstveit et al., 2016; the Kenyan PRIMR/Tusome studies by Piper and colleagues) and, for Liberian school context, Romero, Sandefur & Sandholtz (2020).
- **Discount the benchmarks.** Before repeating the "more than double" comparison (text, p. 11), consider that the test was aligned to the treatment textbooks and the control group received essentially no civics instruction. Cheung & Slavin (2016) and Kraft (2020) explain why such effects run large. Do not repeat the ICCS "467 to 586" range as the full distribution: at least two ICCS 2016 participants scored below 467.
- **Verify these characterizations before repeating them:** that Green et al. (2011), Morduchowicz et al. (1996), and NORC (2019) are HIC studies (pp. 2, 16); that Morduchowicz et al. is a secondary-level randomized evaluation (p. 3); that Nie & Hillygus (2001) and Niemi & Junn (1998) provide longitudinal evidence on childhood knowledge (p. 3); and that Alan et al. (2021) and Dhar et al. (2022) show that such complements are hard to implement in low-resource settings (p. 16).
- **For the behavioral question, read work showing school curricula can shift social and civic behavior in LMICs:** Alan et al. (2021), Dhar et al. (2022), and Friedman et al. (2016). For adult civic education in Africa, see Finkel (2002), Gottlieb (2016), and Mvukiyehe & Samii (2017).
- **Attitude outcomes cannot be compared.** The paper's theory of change includes attitudes (text, p. 7), and attitudes are the central outcome in its closest antecedents (Green et al.; Finkel & Ernst; ICCS). But attitude results are only "available upon request" (note 3, p. 18), and the Supplemental Appendix could not be checked. So readers cannot place the paper against that part of the literature.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Coverage.* The reference list is long (pp. 18-22) and much of it is well chosen for the civic-education side of the question [checkable]. The weakness is the choice of neighbors. For a USAID-funded program delivered through Liberian public schools, the most relevant bodies of evidence are (i) randomized civic and voter education in fragile African states, (ii) structured-pedagogy trials in sub-Saharan primary schools, and (iii) experimental and quasi-experimental work on schooling and political outcomes in Africa. All three are essentially absent [external knowledge]. The omissions matter because each supplies a comparison that changes interpretation.

Adult civic-education RCTs in Liberia and Mali show that the "first experimental evidence" claim is first only for children. Structured-pedagogy trials show that a materials-plus-training-plus-monitoring package producing sizable gains on aligned tests is a familiar result. The education-and-politics literature shows that civic effects of schooling can depend on regime and content (Croke et al., 2016; Cantoni et al., 2017). That point is relevant here, since one of the three engagement items is "I obey the laws in my community" (Table 6, p. 15) [checkable]. The Liberian anchor makes the gap especially visible: the paper cites Blair, Blattman & Hartman (2011) for Liberian social cohesion (text, p. 4) [checkable], but not the randomized community-education trial that grew out of that research program (Blattman, Hartman & Blair, 2014, *APSR*) [external knowledge, high confidence].

*Accuracy of characterization.* Most individual descriptions are serviceable. Glewwe et al. (2009) and Sabarwal et al. (2014) are described fairly [external knowledge, high confidence]. The problems are mostly in how studies are grouped, not what individual studies are said to find.

Three groupings matter. First, labeling Argentina (1990s) and Georgia (2019) as HIC contexts (text, p. 16) props up the paper's framing of an HIC participatory literature against an LMIC textbook result. Second, counting Morduchowicz et al. (1996) as secondary-level (text, p. 3) supports the claim that primary-level experimental work consists only of Mahéo (2018). Published descriptions I found put the Argentine program in 5th/6th-grade classrooms [external knowledge via WebSearch; I could not confirm whether assignment was random]. Third, Green et al. (2011) is presented as an example of the participatory model. Its substantive finding, knowledge up with little change in civil-liberties attitudes, is in fact the closest precedent for this paper's own pattern [external knowledge, fairly high confidence].

The longitudinal-consequence claim on p. 3 also overreaches its citations. Nie & Hillygus (2001) is about the college years, as its title in the reference list says [checkable]. Niemi & Junn (1998) is, as I understand it, a cross-sectional NAEP analysis [external knowledge, moderate-high confidence].

*Novelty.* In its narrow, fully qualified form (school-based civics curriculum, student outcomes, low-income post-conflict country), I cannot name a clear prior RCT, and the claim may well be correct [judgment; limited by my knowledge of grey literature and NGO evaluations]. Two broader framings in the paper are oversold. The first is that the study addresses "the critical lack of experimental research on civic education in any context" (text, p. 3). Donbavand & Hoskins (2021), a systematic review of controlled trials the paper itself cites (p. 7), collects a body of such trials. The US literature also has lottery-based and experimental civic-outcome evidence the paper does not cite, including Gill et al. (2020, *APSR*) on Democracy Prep and Holbein (2017, *APSR*) using the Fast Track elementary-school RCT [external knowledge, high confidence]. The second is that the textbook result offers "new insight" into instructional materials (text, p. 3), which, as argued above, reflects a comparison with textbook-only provision rather than the structured-pedagogy literature [judgment].

The contribution to the literature on classroom instruction in non-core subjects (text, p. 3) is a real gap. But the classroom evidence comes from a Stallings time-use instrument (text, p. 10; Table 5, p. 15) that records materials and engagement rather than rote versus interactive pedagogy. The Teach Primary data were dropped for reliability reasons (note 4, p. 18). So the claim that civics instruction shows "a strong reliance on rote memorization" (text, p. 3) is asserted more than measured [checkable; judgment].

*Conflicting evidence.* The paper selects supporting sources for its pessimism about behavior (Finkel & Ernst, 2005; Manning & Edwards, 2014; Soule, 2002; Hoskins et al., 2021; text pp. 3, 16) and does not engage the evidence that civic and social-behavioral outcomes can move. Finkel's own adult civic-education studies found participation effects in developing democracies, especially with participatory, repeated sessions (Finkel, 2002) [external knowledge, high confidence]. Mvukiyehe & Samii (2017) found shifts in electoral enthusiasm and willingness to report manipulation in Liberia [WebSearch-confirmed]. Alan et al. (2021) and Dhar et al. (2022), both cited, changed behaviors and attitudes through school-delivered curricula in public schools in middle-income countries [external knowledge, high confidence]. Citing those two as evidence that complements are "harder to implement in low-resource settings" (text, p. 16) inverts their main lesson [judgment].

The developmental-psychology explanation for the null (peer norms constrain adult-led instruction; text, p. 16) is post hoc. It draws on literature mostly about peer influence on risk behavior [external knowledge, moderate confidence]. Measurement is the more parsimonious explanation. The outcomes are three self-reported items with control-group endorsement rates of 0.75-0.84 (Table 6, p. 15), which the paper itself flags as a ceiling concern (text, p. 16) [checkable].

On the other side of the knowledge-versus-participation debate, the "knowledge-first" position rests on a single, non-empirical source (Hirsch, 2020; text, p. 2) [checkable]. The empirical skeptics of knowledge-to-participation pathways are not engaged. Holbein & Hillygus (2020) is cited for outcome types only [checkable]. Weinschenk & Dawes (2022, *BJPolS*), which I recall finding little turnout effect of high-school civics coursework, is not cited [external knowledge, moderate confidence].

*Placement in the field.* The paper sits at the junction of political-science work on civic education and development-economics work on LMIC learning interventions. It takes its main framing from the first and its benchmarks from the second. From economics, readers should add the structured-pedagogy and effect-size-interpretation literatures (Cheung & Slavin, 2016; Kraft, 2020), which suggest the 0.38 SD should be read as a gain on a curriculum-aligned test against a no-instruction counterfactual, not as evidence of unusual efficiency. From political science, the regime-dependent and "indoctrination vs. democratic citizenship" work (Croke et al., 2016; Cantoni et al., 2017; Paglayan, 2021, *APSR*) is relevant to how civic curricula in fragile states should be evaluated [external knowledge, high confidence for Croke and Cantoni; moderate-high for Paglayan]. From comparative and international education, the qualitative literature on citizenship and peace education in post-conflict settings, including Liberia, would have grounded the textbook's content and the choice of engagement items. The paper uses only Quaynor (2012) as the source of survey items (text, p. 10) [checkable; external knowledge on the broader literature].

*Limits of this review.* I could not check the Supplemental Appendix, which the paper says contains the theory of change (Table A.1), assessment frameworks (B.2-B.4), and attitude-measure details (B.1). It may address some positioning gaps. I checked four citations by WebSearch: Mvukiyehe & Samii (2017), existence and findings; Gottlieb (2016), existence and design; Morduchowicz et al. (1996), grade level, with randomization unconfirmed; and the ICCS 2016 score range and low-scoring participants. Alan et al. (2021) was also checked for its elementary-school setting. All other named omissions rest on my own knowledge and carry the certainty levels stated inline. I may be missing NGO or grey-literature evaluations of school civic or peace education in low-income African countries that would bear on the "first" claim.
