### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper is short, conventionally organized, and easy to read, and nearly every headline number in the abstract and introduction matches Tables 3, 5, and 6 exactly. But the prose drifts from the exhibits in a few places that matter. One headline instructional-practice number has no exhibit in the paper. The rural-district heterogeneity result is described much more mildly than Table 4 supports. The attrition statement misreads the coefficient it cites, and fidelity statistics shift from section to section. Readers can trust the main treatment-effect numbers as quoted. They should check the heterogeneity, attrition, fidelity, and contextualization claims against the tables themselves.

**Strengths:**

- The paper is short and easy to navigate. The introduction previews all three findings (knowledge, mechanism, engagement) in the same order as the Results section, and every result paragraph points to its table or figure (pp. 2-3, 10-12).
- The core effect sizes are quoted accurately [checkable]. The overall effect of 0.38 SD matches 0.379*** in Table 3, Panel A. Participation (0.36), society and systems (0.28), and knowing (0.37) match 0.364***, 0.284***, and 0.370*** in Table 3, Panels B-C. The null domains (principles 0.091, identities 0.021, reasoning 0.076) are correctly called "smaller and not statistically significant" (text, p. 11).
- The derived contextualizations are arithmetically correct [checkable]. Φ(0.379) = 0.648, so "approximately 15 percentile points" holds (text, p. 11). 0.38/0.15 = 2.53, so "more than double" the upper meta-analytic bound holds (text, p. 11). The Table 6 upper bound for "I obey the laws" is 0.036 + 1.96×0.023 = 0.081, so "rule out effects larger than approximately 8 percentage points" holds (text, p. 12; Table 6, p. 15).
- Sample-flow numbers reconcile [checkable]. 167 − 16 − 4 − 2 = 145 eligible schools, and 44 + 48 + 48 = 140 sampled (text, p. 5). 1,101 + 1,006 = 2,107 at baseline (Table 1). 936 + 848 = 1,784 at endline (Table 3). 936/1,101 = 0.850 matches the Table 2 control mean. 1,784/2,107 = 85% (text, p. 8). 2,107/140 = 15 students per school (text, p. 8).
- Table 5 is internally coherent. Each panel's categories sum to 1.00 in both arms, so readers can read the time shares as a full decomposition of class time (p. 15).
- The paper offers several honest caveats: the meta-analysis comparison is caveated (p. 11), the rural estimate is flagged as using county rather than strata fixed effects (pp. 12, 16), and ceiling effects on engagement are acknowledged (p. 16).

**Weaknesses:**

- **A headline instructional-practice number has no exhibit [checkable].** The text says "students in treatment schools used textbooks for 63% of class time, while students in control schools only used textbooks for 2% of class time (p < .01)" (text, p. 12). The intro says "Students similarly increased their use of textbooks" (p. 3). Table 5 (p. 15) has no student-textbook-use row: Panel B is labeled "(teachers)" and Panel C covers engagement only. Readers cannot verify the 63% vs. 2% figures from the main paper.
- **The rural heterogeneity result is understated in the Discussion and missing from the abstract and intro [checkable → judgment].** Table 4, column 5 (p. 14) reports Treatment −0.177 (0.219) and Interaction 0.706*** (0.238). That implies an effect of −0.18 SD (n.s.) in non-rural districts and about +0.53 SD in rural districts. The Results text correctly quotes 0.706 but describes "substantially stronger gains in rural schools relative to urban schools" (p. 12), which implies urban schools gained. The Discussion calls it "somewhat larger improvements … in rural schools" and "broadly shared across students" (p. 16). The Discussion and Conclusion then say "across a diverse student body" (p. 17) and "across a broad range of students" (p. 17). With the paper's own caveat about the fixed-effect substitution, the table shows no urban-district gain at the point estimate. That is the single largest heterogeneity finding, and neither the abstract nor the intro results preview (pp. 1-3) mentions it.
- **The attrition sentence misreads Table 2 [checkable].** The text says "Older students in the treatment group were slightly less likely to be reassessed … with the likelihood of reassessment decreasing by about 1.5 percentage points for each year of age. Although this difference is statistically significant…" (p. 8). In Table 2, Panel B (p. 9), −0.015* (0.008) is the Age × Treatment *interaction*, meaning the gap relative to control's age gradient. The within-treatment age gradient is −0.008 + (−0.015) = −0.023, or about 2.3 pp per year. The coefficient is also significant only at 10% (p ≈ .06), which "statistically significant" does not convey. The text never mentions the Panel B Treatment main effect, 0.183* (0.107), which is an extrapolation to age 0.
- **Fidelity statistics change between sections, and none has an exhibit [checkable].** The intro says "100% of teachers and 96% of students receiv[ed] new civic education textbooks" (p. 2). The fidelity section instead says principals "confirmed that textbooks reached 100% of treatment *schools*" (p. 7). The fidelity section says "96% of students confirming receipt" (p. 7), but the Discussion upgrades that to "96% of students receiving *and regularly using* the materials" (p. 17). No table in the main paper reports the fidelity measures (100%, 96%, 94%, 94%, 38 minutes, 29/48).
- **The outcome metric is defined inconsistently [checkable].** The Data section says IRT scores "are standardized to have mean zero and SD one at baseline" (p. 10). Table 3's note says "All scores are standardized to have mean zero and SD one in the control group," and the endline control row is exactly 0.000 [1.000] (p. 11). Table 1 shows the baseline treatment mean at 0.043 [1.075] (p. 6), which also implies control-group rather than pooled standardization. This matters because the ICCS and meta-analysis conversions depend on what "1 SD" means.
- **"All analyses" overstates the covariate set [checkable].** The text says "All analyses control for students' baseline assessment scores in all program effect calculations" (p. 10). The Table 5 note lists only randomization strata (p. 15), and the Table 6 note lists baseline civic engagement, not assessment scores (p. 15). The same page promises heterogeneity by "teacher, and school covariates" (p. 10), but Table 4 has no teacher covariates.
- **Contextualization rests on unstated assumptions [judgment].** The ICCS "38-point" conversion (p. 11) is arithmetically consistent (482 + 38 = 520, just above 517). But it silently assumes 1 SD on this grade-3/4, single-country, control-group-standardized, curriculum-aligned test equals 100 ICCS points. The paper never states that assumption, and the ICCS values (24 countries, 482, 517, 467-586) cannot be checked within the paper. The meta-analysis caveat (p. 11) mentions only the subject-matter difference. It does not mention that the outcome test was aligned to textbooks only the treatment group received, which likely inflates the comparison.
- **Mechanism language outruns the observation data [judgment].** "Classroom observations suggest that these knowledge gains were driven by textbook-centered instruction" (pp. 2-3) is a causal-channel claim built on a descriptive 60-school observation (Table 5). The claim that civic instruction shows "a strong reliance on rote memorization" (p. 3) has no corresponding measure in any exhibit.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- To get the core finding, read the abstract, pp. 10-12 (Results), and Table 3 (p. 11). You can quote the Table 3 numbers and the intro/abstract effect sizes as written.
- Do not skip Table 4, column 5 (p. 14). Compute the implied effects yourself: about −0.18 SD in non-rural districts and about +0.53 SD in rural districts. The prose ("somewhat larger," "broadly shared," "across a diverse student body") does not convey that pattern. Before citing the result as general, also weigh the paper's own caution about replacing strata fixed effects with county fixed effects.
- Read Figure 1 (p. 13) with its confidence bands in view. The difference line is positive throughout, so "positive effects across the achievement distribution" (abstract) is true of point estimates. But the lower 95% band crosses zero at roughly the top fifth of the endline distribution (Panel A) and the top few percent of the baseline distribution (Panel B), readings approximate from the plot. The text concedes this only in a parenthetical (p. 12).
- Do not cite the student textbook-use figures (63% vs. 2%, p. 12) or any fidelity percentage (pp. 2, 7, 17) as table-verified. They appear only in prose, and the fidelity figures shift between sections. Cite the p. 7 wording ("confirming receipt"), not the p. 17 wording ("receiving and regularly using").
- For the attrition discussion, go straight to Table 2, Panel B (p. 9). The 1.5 pp figure is a differential, not the treatment-group age gradient, and it is significant only at 10%.
- Treat the ICCS and meta-analysis comparisons (p. 11) as illustrative. The arithmetic checks out, but the scale equivalence is assumed, not shown.
- For the engagement null, Table 6 supports "no detectable effect." The index 95% CI is about [−0.026, +0.032], and no item bound exceeds about 8 pp. Note that "helping other students" has a negative point estimate (−0.034, 95% CI ≈ [−0.075, +0.007]), which the text does not mention. The claim that baseline engagement levels "were already high" (p. 16) has no baseline exhibit; the endline control means of 0.75-0.84 are the closest proxy.
- Anything the paper points to in the online Supplemental Appendix could not be checked: baseline distributions (Fig. A.2), theory of change (Table A.1), instrument details (B.1-B.5), and attitude outcomes (fn. 3).
- You can skim the Context section (pp. 4-5) and the literature paragraphs of the Discussion (pp. 16-17) without losing anything needed to evaluate the evidence.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Organization and navigability.* The paper follows a standard, efficient structure: intro with results preview, Experiment, Data, Empirical Strategy, Results, Discussion, Conclusion. It carries six tables and one figure. The load-bearing exhibits are Table 3 (main effects), Figure 1 and Table 4 (distribution and heterogeneity), Table 5 (the "mechanism" story), and Table 6 (the engagement null). Each results paragraph cites its exhibit, which makes the paper easy to audit. Three navigability gaps stand out. First, the paper never tells the reader which outcomes and subgroups were pre-registered, even though a pre-analysis plan exists (fn. 5, p. 18). The rural-district split is the only significant heterogeneity result, so knowing whether it was pre-specified matters for how much weight it gets. Second, the unit of observation in Table 5 is labeled "N (schools)" (30/30), while the methods describe outcomes "measured at the classroom level" (p. 10). Readers cannot tell how many classrooms per school were observed. Third, several Table 5 labels overlap: "10 or more students engaged" and "2–10 students engaged" both include 10, and "all students engaged" versus "10 or more" is undefined for small classes. [checkable, minor]

*Fidelity of argument.* The main-effect prose is disciplined. The drift appears in secondary findings and in the Discussion's synthesis. The clearest case is rural heterogeneity. Table 4, column 5 implies the effect is concentrated in rural districts, with a negative (n.s.) point estimate elsewhere. The narrative instead moves from "substantially stronger gains in rural schools relative to urban schools" (p. 12) to "somewhat larger improvements" and "broadly shared" (p. 16), and then to "across a diverse student body" and "across a broad range of students" (p. 17). That is a progressive softening of a result that, taken at face value, limits the paper's generalization claims. The Discussion's generalization paragraph (p. 17) names countries by conflict history and resource level. It never mentions that the program's measured effect may be confined to rural districts, which is the most direct generalization-relevant finding in the paper [judgment]. The distributional prose adds a second, smaller overreach. It says Panel A shows that "medium-performing students at baseline *and endline* saw the largest gains" (p. 12). Quantile treatment effects on the endline distribution do not identify gains for particular students, and the inverted-U pattern is cited as "consistent with" a linear interaction of −0.058 (n.s., Table 4 col. 6), which cannot detect curvature [judgment]. "First-order stochastically dominates" (p. 12) is a population claim, while Figure 1 shows point estimates with bands that include zero at the top. Its "at every percentile" phrasing should be read as a statement about point estimates [judgment].

The instructional-practices narrative is mostly faithful to Table 5: 57% vs. 15%, 49.6% vs. 24.9%, ~77% learning time, 15-17% management, 6-8% off-task, and 87% vs. 71% all-engaged all match. But "students also became more engaged with the teacher" (p. 12) and "increasing classroom engagement" (p. 16) oversell what Panel C shows. The "no students engaged" share is essentially unchanged (0.054 vs. 0.037; −0.004, n.s.). The gain comes from a shift from "2–10 students engaged" (−0.132***) to "all students engaged" (+0.146**), so the measure moved from small-group to whole-class engagement, not from disengagement to engagement. The paper's own final phrase, "higher whole-class engagement" (p. 12), is the accurate one [checkable → judgment]. Calling time use "broadly in line with established 'good practice' time-use benchmarks" (p. 12) cannot be checked because the paper does not state the benchmark value. From outside this paper, the Stallings/Bruns & Luque benchmark is commonly cited as about 85% of time on learning, which ~77% falls below. Readers should verify this against the cited source [judgment; relies on knowledge outside the paper]. The fidelity prose ("adhered closely," "38 minutes, just under the targeted 45," monitoring "occurred frequently" with 29 of 48 reporting 2-4 visits) is generous: 38/45 = 84% of target, and 29/48 = 60% of interviewees [checkable arithmetic; characterization is judgment].

*Abstract fidelity.* The abstract's numbers match Table 3: 0.38 = 0.379, and 0.37 = 0.370 for knowing. "Positive effects across the achievement distribution" is accurate for point estimates but omits the loss of significance at the top. "No impact on students' civic engagement" would be more precise as "no detectable impact on three self-reported behaviors." The abstract also omits the content-domain split (two of four domains), the null on reasoning (0.076, n.s.), and the rural concentration. "140 schools serving grades 3 and 4" slightly misdescribes the design: schools serve grades 1-6, all of which were treated (p. 5), and only grades 3-4 were evaluated.

*Internal consistency, smaller items.* (i) "8% of control school principals (6 out of 70)" (pp. 5-6): 6/70 = 8.6%, which rounds to 9%. The same sentence's 8/70 = 11.4% → "11%" is fine [checkable, trivial]. (ii) "140 schools … represents approximately 16% of public primary schools across the three counties" (p. 5) implies roughly 875 schools, but the same paragraph calls the sampling frame "167 public primary schools in the counties." How the 167 were drawn from the larger universe is never explained [checkable → exposition gap]. (iii) The class-size eligibility rule (15-40 per class, p. 5) appears in no exclusion count, and the tallied exclusions (16 + 4 + 2) account fully for 167 → 145. (iv) Table 1 reports regression-adjusted differences (with strata FE), which differ slightly from raw mean differences, for example IRT 0.029 vs. a raw 0.043. That is standard, but a reader comparing columns should know the Difference column is not column 2 minus column 1 (p. 6).

*Compact list of text-vs-exhibit checks (all tables and Figure 1 verified on rendered PDF pages).*

The rating is held to Adequate by the concentration of problems in exactly the claims a policy reader would carry away: generality across students and settings, implementation fidelity, and the "textbook-centered instruction drove the gains" story. In each case, the prose either lacks an exhibit or reads more favorably than the exhibit. The online Supplemental Appendix was not available, so any resolution it might provide (e.g., a student-textbook-use table or fidelity tables) could not be checked.

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper reports a well-executed, 140-school RCT showing that adding a USAID-funded civics program to grades 3-4 in Liberia raised scores on a curriculum-aligned civic knowledge test by 0.38 SD after one year. The gain was concentrated in factual recall, with no detectable effect on reasoning, on the "civic identities" (peace and inter-group) domain, or on three self-reported prosocial behaviors. This is valuable evidence from a setting where rigorous school-based civics evidence is very scarce. But the claims most likely to be quoted ("textbook-centered civic education works," a "scalable model for strengthening democratic foundations in fragile states," a new lesson for the textbook-provision literature) go well beyond what the evidence supports: a bundled program that introduced a subject most control schools did not teach, tested with an instrument written to match that subject.

**Strengths:**

- **Rare setting and a clean design.** The study randomized 140 schools (70/70, stratified by county and district), and balance is good (joint F p = .444; Table 1, p. 6). Attrition is 15% and not differential by arm (−0.006, SE 0.020; Table 2 Panel A, p. 9). Implementation fidelity is documented: textbooks reached 100% of treatment schools and 96% of students, and teacher training had 94% participation (text, p. 7). [checkable] RCT evidence on school-based civic education for primary-age children in a low-income, conflict-affected country is genuinely scarce. [external knowledge]
- **Credible, precisely estimated knowledge effect.** The effect is 0.379 SD (SE 0.086; Table 3 Panel A, p. 11). The treatment distribution dominates the control distribution across quantiles (Figure 1 Panel A, p. 13), and there is no heterogeneity by gender, grade, SES, or home language (Table 4, p. 14). [checkable] As evidence that students in this system learn curricular civics content when it is actually delivered, the result is solid. [judgment]
- **Informative decomposition that the authors report candidly.** Gains are in "knowing" (0.370, SE 0.078) and not in "reasoning and applying" (0.076, SE 0.085; Table 3 Panel C, p. 11). Gains are in society/systems and participation, not in principles or identities (Table 3 Panel B). The abstract reports the null on engagement. [checkable] This is more honest than a single headline number would be, and the "knowing vs. reasoning" split is the paper's most useful substantive finding. [judgment]
- **Feasibility evidence.** Delivering individual take-home textbooks and running a regular twice-weekly timetabled subject in this system is itself informative for implementers (text, pp. 7-8; Table 5 Panel B, p. 15). [checkable/judgment]
- **A precisely estimated null on the chosen engagement items.** The index effect is 0.003 (SE 0.015; Table 6, p. 15), and the paper rules out effects larger than about 8 percentage points on the "obey laws" item (text, p. 12). [checkable]

**Weaknesses:**

- **The counterfactual is "no civics," not "other civics."** Only 6 of 70 control principals reported teaching civics (text, pp. 5-6), so the estimate is the effect of introducing a subject, with its own curriculum, time slot, books, training, and monitoring, on a test of that subject's content. The assessment was "aligned with the Grade 3 and Grade 4 Liberian civic education curriculum" (text, p. 8), and the program's textbooks "provided a concrete formulation of what teachers were expected to cover" (text, p. 7). [checkable] A large effect under these conditions is expected, so it tells us less about civic education's efficacy than "0.38 SD" suggests. [judgment]
- **The benchmarks overstate the effect.** The paper compares 0.38 SD with LMIC meta-analytic means of 0.08-0.15 SD (text, p. 11) and translates it into a 38-point ICCS gain equal to moving "from Colombia (482) to just above the international average (517)" (text, p. 11). [checkable] The meta-analysis comparison is hedged. The ICCS conversion is not. It assumes one SD among baseline Liberian 3rd/4th graders equals the ICCS cross-national SD of 100 among 14-year-olds, and nothing supports that. Both benchmarks also mix aligned tests of new content with general achievement tests. [judgment] There is also a minor inconsistency about the reference SD: baseline standardization (p. 10) versus control-group endline standardization (Table 3 note, p. 11). [checkable]
- **The four-component bundle cannot support the textbook contribution.** Contribution 3 (p. 3) and the policy discussion (pp. 16-17) set these results against textbook-provision nulls (Glewwe et al., 2009; Sabarwal et al., 2014). They conclude that aligned, well-integrated materials "can significantly enhance learning." [checkable] Here textbooks came with new instructional time, a new subject, training, and twice-monthly monitoring (p. 6), so the design cannot separate the materials from everything else. The comparison is also not like-for-like: the earlier studies added books to subjects already being taught. [judgment; external knowledge on the Kenya/Sierra Leone designs]
- **The domain most tied to the post-conflict rationale did not move.** The civic identities domain covers "relations across tribes and religions, and peace-promoting attitudes and behaviors" (text, p. 9), and its estimate is 0.021 (SE 0.067; Table 3 Panel B). The paper uses post-conflict social cohesion as its motivation (pp. 1-2, 4) and ends by calling the program a model "for strengthening democratic foundations in fragile states" (p. 17), yet this null goes undiscussed. [checkable; judgment]
- **The rural result is understated, which matters for generalizability.** In Table 4 column 5 (p. 14), the treatment coefficient for non-rural districts is −0.177 (SE 0.219), with a rural interaction of 0.706 (SE 0.238). The implied rural effect is about 0.53 SD, and the urban effect cannot be distinguished from zero. [checkable] The paper calls this "somewhat larger improvements" (p. 16) and elsewhere says gains were "broadly shared" and held "across a diverse student body" (pp. 16-17). The specification departs from the randomization strata (county fixed effects; p. 12), and the number of district-level clusters behind "rural" is not reported. So this finding is fragile, but it cuts against an unconditional headline. [judgment]
- **The engagement null has limited reach.** The measure is three self-reported items, dichotomized into "always/often" (Table 6 note). Control means are 0.75-0.84 (Table 6), and the paper itself raises possible ceiling effects (p. 16). The items (helping peers, helping neighbors, obeying laws) are prosocial conduct more than civic or political engagement. [checkable; judgment] The paper's conclusion that "content delivery alone is unlikely to shift behavior in this age group" (p. 16), and its peer-norm developmental explanation, rest on a thin measure. [judgment]
- **Attitude outcomes are missing from the paper.** The theory of change runs from knowledge to attitudes to behaviors (p. 7), but attitude results are "available upon request" (note 3, p. 18). A pedagogy tool (Teach Primary) was dropped for reliability reasons (note 4). The pre-analysis plan was first published June 24, 2024 (note 5), which is after baseline (start of the 2023-24 school year; p. 8) and plausibly near endline. [checkable] Readers cannot see from the paper which outcomes were pre-specified as primary. The Supplemental Appendix B.1 and the registry could not be checked.
- **The novelty claim is stated more broadly in the conclusion than in the introduction.** The introduction limits the first-evidence claim to "student civic outcomes" (p. 2). The conclusion drops that limit: "the first experimental evidence on the effectiveness of civic education in a low-income, post-conflict setting" (p. 17). [checkable] RCTs of adult civic and voter education exist in low-income and post-conflict settings, including in Liberia itself (e.g., Blattman, Hartman & Blair, 2014; Mvukiyehe & Samii, 2017) and in Mali (Gottlieb, 2016). The unqualified version is therefore inaccurate as far as I know. [external knowledge]

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Cite it for this:** a curriculum-plus-materials civics program in grades 3-4 in Liberia raised scores on a curriculum-aligned civic knowledge test by about 0.38 SD after one year (Table 3), mainly through factual recall ("knowing" 0.37 SD). It had no detectable effect on reasoning or application (0.08 SD, ns).
- **Cite it for this:** feasibility. Individual textbooks and a regular twice-weekly civics slot can be delivered with high fidelity in a low-resource West African system, and doing so sharply shifts classroom materials use (Table 5 Panel B).
- **Cite it for this, with care:** a precisely estimated null on three self-reported, textbook-targeted prosocial behaviors within one school year (Table 6). Describe these as prosocial self-reports near ceiling, not as civic or political engagement generally.
- **Do not cite it as showing that "textbook-centered civic education works" relative to participatory approaches.** No participatory arm was tested, and the knowledge-first debate (Hirsch; p. 2) is not adjudicated.
- **Do not cite it as evidence that textbooks improve learning, or as resolving the textbook-provision puzzle.** Textbooks were one of four bundled components, and the counterfactual lacked the subject entirely.
- **Do not cite it for effects on social cohesion, peace attitudes, democratic values, or "democratic foundations."** The identities domain effect is about zero, and attitude results are not reported.
- **Do not cite the 0.38 SD as comparable to general achievement effects** (e.g., "double the LMIC average") **or as a 38-point ICCS gain.** The test is aligned to a curriculum that controls did not receive, and the SD scales are not equivalent.
- **Do not cite it as "the first experimental evidence on civic education in a low-income, post-conflict setting"** without the "school-based, student outcomes" qualifier.
- **Open questions:** whether the knowledge gains persist; which component drives them; whether gains appear on an independent, non-aligned civics measure; whether effects hold in urban schools, given the rural/urban split in Table 4; what the attitude results show; what the program costs relative to alternatives; and whether early knowledge gains translate into later civic participation.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*What is genuinely new.* The paper supplies experimental evidence where there was almost none: school-based civic instruction for primary-grade (though heavily over-age, mean age about 13; Table 1) students in a low-income, post-conflict African country. [checkable; external knowledge] Its design strengths are real: school-level randomization within strata, 140 clusters, low and balanced attrition, IRT scaling with common items, a distributional analysis, and classroom observations that document what "treatment" meant in practice. The main result is therefore credible as an internal-validity matter. What the paper adds beyond "it worked" is the knowledge profile. Gains appear where the textbook conveys facts about institutions and participation, and not in reasoning, principles, or identities (Table 3). This specificity is the paper's best-supported and most useful finding, and it deserves more weight than the headline number. [judgment]

*What the 0.38 SD actually estimates.* Two features of the design shape the interpretation. First, control schools largely did not teach civics at all (pp. 5-6). Second, the test was built from the ICCS framework but "aligned with" the treatment curriculum (p. 8). [checkable] The estimand is therefore closest to the effect of receiving instruction in a body of content on a test of that content, relative to not receiving it. Seen that way, a sizeable effect on recall of taught material is close to a manipulation check on delivery. [judgment] The more informative results are the ones at or near zero. A year of textbook-based civics did not move students' ability to apply concepts, and it did not move the "identities" content (inter-group relations, peace) that is most closely tied to the post-conflict case for the program. [checkable; judgment] The meta-analytic and ICCS comparisons (p. 11) treat the effect as though it were a general achievement gain, and readers should discount them accordingly. The meta-analysis comparison carries a caveat. The ICCS translation carries none, although it rests on an unsupported equivalence of standard deviations across very different populations and instruments. [judgment]

*Contribution claims versus evidence.* The paper claims three contributions (pp. 3-4). The first (an experiment where few exist) is well supported, subject to the scoping note on novelty below. The second (a contribution to the instruction literature, showing that civics teaching resembles math and language teaching in its "strong reliance on rote memorization and teacher-centered methods") rests on a Stallings-style time-use and materials instrument in 60 schools at endline only (p. 10; Table 5). [checkable] That instrument records materials and time on task, not the cognitive demand of instruction, and the tool that would have measured pedagogy was dropped for reliability reasons (note 4, p. 18). The main text also does not say which lessons were observed in control classrooms that had no civics period, so the treatment-control contrast in Table 5 may compare a civics lesson with some other subject. The Supplemental Appendix could not be checked on this point. [checkable; judgment] Contribution 2 is therefore more descriptive than the framing suggests. The third contribution (on textbook effectiveness) is the least supported. The bundle cannot isolate materials. The explanations the paper offers for the contrast with Kenya and Sierra Leone (contextual tailoring, utilization, structured delivery; p. 17) are plausible, but they are post hoc and untested within this design. [judgment]

*Most quotable versus best supported.* The abstract is fairly disciplined. The quotable sentences sit in the discussion and conclusion: civic education "can be effectively implemented in resource-constrained settings without requiring fundamental shifts in pedagogy, making knowledge-building programs more scalable and sustainable" (p. 16), and textbook-centered programs offer "a scalable model for strengthening democratic foundations in fragile states" (p. 17). [checkable] "Scalable" is asserted, not shown. The paper reports no costs, delivery ran through donor-funded NGOs with twice-monthly monitoring, and the authors themselves note that monitoring may be hard to sustain at scale (p. 17). [checkable] Whether the donor-dependent delivery model can continue at all in the post-2025 aid environment is an open practical question the paper, reasonably, does not address. [external knowledge; judgment] "Strengthening democratic foundations" has no support in the outcomes. Behaviors did not move, identities did not move, and attitudes are not reported (note 3). [checkable] The best-supported one-line summary is narrower: *introducing a structured, textbook-based civics curriculum raised primary students' factual civic knowledge in a low-resource post-conflict system but did not, within a year, change reasoning, identity-related knowledge, or self-reported prosocial behavior.* [judgment]

*Generalizability and boundary-drawing.* The explicit generalizability paragraph (p. 17) is better than most. It names the three features of Liberia (post-conflict, fragile democracy, severe material constraints) and candidate replication sites. [checkable] Two points qualify it. First, the sample is restricted to schools accessible within 4 hours, with class sizes of 15-40, in three purposively chosen counties (p. 5). Second, and more important, the internal heterogeneity suggests the effect may depend heavily on setting. Urban-district effects are indistinguishable from zero (−0.177, SE 0.219), while rural effects are large (Table 4, col. 5). [checkable] The authors rightly flag the change of fixed effects needed to estimate this, and the district-level definition of rurality leaves few effective clusters. Still, "somewhat larger" (p. 16) undersells a contrast that, if real, would bear directly on where such a program is worth funding. It also sits awkwardly with the claim of gains "across a diverse student body" (p. 17). [judgment] Nothing in the design identifies whether post-conflict status itself moderates effects, so "post-conflict" describes the setting rather than any mechanism the study established. [judgment]

*Standing in the literature.* I read the introduction's novelty claim (p. 2: first experimental evaluation "of a civic education program's effects on student civic outcomes in a low-income, post-conflict context") as defensible, and the paper hedges it with "to our knowledge." [checkable; external knowledge] The conclusion's broader restatement is not defensible, given adult civic- and voter-education field experiments in Liberia and elsewhere in West Africa. [external knowledge] The statement that civic education lacks experimental research "in any context" (p. 3) also sits uneasily with the paper's own citation of a systematic review of controlled trials (Donbavand & Hoskins, 2021; p. 7). [checkable] Within its proper scope, this is likely now the best causal evidence on whether primary-level civics instruction raises civic knowledge in a low-income sub-Saharan system. It is not strong evidence on civic engagement, attitudes, pedagogy comparisons, or textbook effects as such. [judgment]

*What it sets up.* The most valuable follow-on work would do four things. It would add a non-aligned or independently developed civic knowledge measure, such as released ICCS or other external items, to separate curriculum coverage from broader civic learning. It would vary components, such as textbooks alone versus textbooks plus monitoring, and cost them. It would follow the cohort to test whether factual gains persist and whether they eventually translate into attitudes or participation. And it would investigate the rural/urban split with a design powered for it. Publishing the attitude results and pre-registered outcome list would let readers judge the full outcome profile now. [judgment]

*Calibration.* The paper makes a modest, rigorous contribution to an important and under-studied question, and it deserves to be cited. The rating is Adequate rather than Strong because the paper's framing of its contribution, especially on textbooks, scalability, democratic foundations, and first-evidence status, goes beyond the evidence in ways readers are likely to reproduce. It is not Weak because the core finding is clear, credible, and honestly decomposed in the tables.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper states its headline intent-to-treat model clearly (Eq. 1, p.10), and its sample counts agree with each other across Tables 1-3. So a reader can understand what was estimated. What a reader cannot do is verify it. The PDF has no data availability statement, no replication package or code statement, and no software named anywhere. The IRT scoring behind the 0.38 SD headline is described in only three sentences, and the paper gives two different standardization conventions for it. Two outcome families that were collected are reported only "upon request." The "pre-analysis plan" was first published June 24, 2024 (fn. 5, p.18), long after baseline data collection at the start of the 2023-24 school year (p.8). The registry lists civic attitudes as a primary outcome, and the paper does not report them.

**Strengths:**

- The headline specification can be read off the page. Eq. 1 (p.10) regresses the endline outcome on the baseline outcome, randomization-stratum fixed effects, and a school-level treatment indicator, estimated by OLS with standard errors clustered by school. The table notes restate the controls for each exhibit (Tables 3-6, pp.11, 14-15) [checkable].
- Sample flow can be checked, and it holds together. 167 − 16 − 4 − 2 = 145 eligible schools, and 44 + 48 + 48 = 140 selected (text, p.5). 2,107 students at baseline is about 15 per school (Table 1, p.6; text, p.8). The control follow-up rate of 0.850 (Table 2, Panel A, p.9) times 1,101 baseline control students gives the 936 control students in Table 3 (p.11). Treatment follow-up is 848/1,006 = 0.843, which matches the −0.006 treatment coefficient on follow-up (Table 2, Panel A) [checkable].
- Attrition gets a full table: a treatment-by-covariate follow-up regression with a joint F-test (F = 1.178, p = .323; Table 2, Panel B, p.9). The age-by-treatment interaction is disclosed openly (−0.015; text, p.8) [checkable].
- The tables report control means and SDs, strata-adjusted differences, clustered SEs, and Ns. The proportion rows in Table 5 sum to 1.00 within each panel, which confirms the categories are exhaustive (p.15) [checkable].
- The engagement coding is stated exactly: 4-point items are dichotomized as always/often versus rarely/never, and the index is the mean of three binaries (Table 6 note, p.15). The paper also names the instrument sources (Quaynor 2012; Stallings/World Bank 2015; ICCS framework; pp.8-10) [checkable].
- The paper gives the power calculation parameters (fn. 1, p.18), the IRB protocol number (p.18), and the registry ID (fn. 5, p.18). All three can be looked up independently [checkable].

**Weaknesses:**

- The PDF contains no data availability statement, no code or replication-package statement, and no named software (Stata, R, or any IRT package). A search of the full text for "code," "replication," "Stata," "software," "repository," and "available" finds only the supplemental-material line, which says "available online," and two "available upon request" footnotes (p.18) [checkable]. The student-level data are USAID-funded evaluation data, not administrative records. A de-identified release or a documented access route was therefore plausible, and the paper does not explain why there is none [judgment].
- The timing of the registration undercuts calling this a pre-registered study. Fn. 5 (p.18) dates the pre-analysis plan's first publication to June 24, 2024. Baseline data were collected at the start of the 2023-24 school year, and endline "near the end of that same school year" (p.8) [checkable]. The paper gives no actual fieldwork dates. A reader therefore cannot tell from the paper whether registration came before or after endline data collection [checkable]. The registry (see Detailed Commentary) lists initial registration on June 14, 2024, and an intervention period of September 25, 2023 to June 24, 2024. Registration came roughly nine months after the program and baseline began [checkable, registry]. The paper does not disclose this gap [checkable].
- A registered primary outcome is missing from the paper. As fetched, the registry lists "student civic knowledge, student civic attitudes, student civic behaviors" as primary outcomes. The paper reports attitudes only "upon request" (fn. 3, p.18), and the main text never describes the attitude measures [checkable]. A second instrument, an adapted Teach Primary observation tool, was also collected and then dropped for "reliability concerns," with results "available upon request" (fn. 4, p.18) [checkable]. Both reasons for the omissions point to Supplemental Appendix B.1, which could not be checked.
- The effect-size units are ambiguous. The text says IRT scores are "standardized to have mean zero and SD one at baseline" (p.10). The Table 3 note says "All scores are standardized to have mean zero and SD one in the control group," and the endline control mean and SD are exactly 0.000 [1.000] (Table 3, p.11). Table 1's baseline control row is also 0.000 [1.000], while the treatment group is 0.043 [1.075] (p.6). That pattern implies standardization against the baseline control group, not the full baseline sample [checkable]. So the 0.379 in Table 3 appears to be in endline-control SD units, which contradicts the p.10 description. A replicator would have to guess which rescaling produces 0.379 [judgment].
- The IRT scoring is thinly documented. The paper does not report the number of items per wave, the number of shared linking items, the estimation method or software, how thetas were scored (e.g., EAP or ML), item fit, or reliability. For the percent-correct subscales, which carry the "knowing" (0.370) and content-domain results in Table 3 (p.11), it does not report item counts per domain, only that items are too few for IRT (p.10). Appendix B.4 is said to contain only "representative items" (p.9) [checkable].
- The sampling and construction steps leave a replicator to guess at the following [checkable]:
  - The class-size eligibility rule (15-40 students, p.5) is stated, but none of the 22 exclusions are attributed to it.
  - The number of eligible schools in each of Montserrado and Nimba is not given (p.5).
  - The number of county-district strata is not given (pp.5, 10).
  - The number of distinct classrooms is not given, even though grades 3 and 4 are sometimes combined (the "280 classrooms" on p.5 conflicts with p.8).
  - How within-class students were sampled, and how a shortfall in one grade was filled from the other, is only loosely described (p.8).
  - How the household assets index used in Tables 2 and 4 was built from the nine items in Table 1 is not described.
  - How "rural district" is defined, and how many schools are rural, is not reported (Table 4, col. 5, p.14; text, p.12).
  - The paper does not say which classroom(s) were observed in the 60-school subsample. Table 5 reports N = 30/30/60 schools with SEs "clustered at the school level" (p.15).
- Some claims in the text do not appear in any exhibit in the PDF [checkable]:
  - Student textbook use of 63% vs. 2% of class time (text, p.12; Table 5 has only teacher-material rows).
  - Baseline engagement levels described as "already high" (text, p.16; Table 6 shows only endline means).
  - Fidelity figures (96% textbook receipt, 94% take-home, 94% training participation; p.7).
  - Heterogeneity by "teacher" covariates, promised on p.10 but absent from Table 4.
- The Figure 1 estimator is not specified enough to rerun it. The note says local polynomial regressions with "bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals" (p.13) but gives no kernel, bandwidth, polynomial order, number of replications, resampling unit (student or school cluster), or seed [checkable].
- Eq. 1 is inconsistent with some of the tables. The text says "All analyses control for students' baseline assessment scores" (p.10). The Table 5 note lists only strata controls, and the Table 6 note lists baseline engagement, not baseline scores (p.15) [checkable]. Table 4, column 5 replaces strata fixed effects with county fixed effects (p.14), an ad hoc departure that the paper acknowledges (p.12) [checkable].

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat the 0.38 SD headline (Table 3, Panel A, p.11) as clearly specified but not independently verifiable. No data, code, item parameters, or scoring script is available. Before comparing it to other effect sizes (e.g., the ICCS conversion on p.11 or the meta-analytic benchmarks), ask the authors which standardization produced 0.379: baseline sample, baseline control, or endline control.
- Do not read fn. 5 as a guarantee against specification search. The registration came well after baseline (p.8; registry). Treat these as exploratory rather than confirmatory: the subscale breakdown, the binarization of engagement (Table 6), and especially the rural-district interaction of 0.706 (Table 4, col. 5), which uses non-standard fixed effects and an undefined rural classification. Ask for the registered analysis plan document and compare its outcomes and heterogeneity dimensions with what was reported.
- Request the civic attitudes results (fn. 3), a registered primary outcome, and the Teach Primary results (fn. 4) before concluding that the program's effects are limited to knowledge. As published, the "no engagement effect" conclusion covers only the three behavior items in Table 6.
- Ask for, or look in the supplement for, the items with domain and cognitive-domain assignments, the list of linking items, the 2PL item parameters, and the software used. The "knowing vs. reasoning" contrast (0.370 vs. 0.076; Table 3, Panel C) depends entirely on an item classification that the PDF does not document.
- USAID-funded evaluations have historically been expected to deposit data with USAID's Development Data Library. A would-be replicator should check there and contact the corresponding author (p.1). The paper itself names no access route [judgment about likely location; not verified].
- The engagement index in Table 6 has the same Ns (936/848) as the knowledge sample. Confirm whether the sample was restricted to students with both test scores, and how missing survey items were handled.
- For the classroom-observation results (Table 5), ask which classroom per school was observed and whether observers were blind to treatment status. As reported, these are 60 school-level observations whose unit of analysis is not stated.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Data and code availability.* I searched the extracted text of all 22 pages and inspected the rendered p.1 and p.18. The article has no data availability statement, no code or replication-package statement, no repository link or DOI for data, no open-science badge, and no mention of the software used for the regressions, the 2PL IRT model, the local polynomial quantile plots, or the bootstrap [checkable]. The only availability language is "Supplemental material for this article is available online" and two "available upon request" footnotes about unreported outcomes (p.18) [checkable]. The online supplement (Figures A.1-A.2, Table A.1, Appendices B.1-B.5) was not available to me, and I cannot say whether it contains instruments or code. These data were collected by the research team under a USAID contract (Funding, p.18). They are not restricted administrative records, and the IRB (ACRE, University of Liberia, Protocol #23-05-368; p.18) is the kind of body that commonly permits de-identified release. The absence of any statement is therefore a real gap, not a legitimate constraint [judgment]. Credit should be modest. A clear specification without data or code lets a reader understand the analysis but not verify it.

*Specification transparency.* The core ITT model is well stated (Eq. 1, p.10). The estimand is the effect of the offer, not scaled to treatment-on-the-treated because dosage is unobserved (p.10), and inference is clustered at the school level. The table notes consistently restate controls and clustering [checkable]. The weaker parts are the edges. The general statement that "all analyses control for students' baseline assessment scores" (p.10) does not match the notes for Table 5 (strata only) or Table 6 (baseline engagement) (p.15) [checkable]. The number of county-district strata, which matters for degrees of freedom with 140 clusters, is never given (pp.5, 10) [checkable]. The rural interaction swaps strata fixed effects for county fixed effects (Table 4 note, p.14). The authors flag this themselves (pp.12, 16). But because "rural district" is never defined and the count of rural schools is not reported, the paper's most striking heterogeneity result cannot be rebuilt [checkable]. Its treatment main effect of −0.177 (0.219) implies a null or negative urban effect, so the definition matters [judgment].

*Outcome construction.* The knowledge outcome is a 2PL IRT score estimated on pooled baseline and endline responses and linked through shared items (p.10). The paper reports none of the quantities a replicator would need: item counts, number of linking items, item parameters, estimation method, theta scoring, reliability, or differential item functioning across waves [checkable]. The standardization discrepancy is the most consequential checkable inconsistency. On p.10 scores are standardized "at baseline." In the Table 3 note (p.11) they are standardized "in the control group," and the endline control mean and SD are exactly 0.000 and 1.000. Table 1 (p.6) shows the baseline control group at 0.000 [1.000] and treatment at 0.043 [1.075]. This fits standardization against the baseline control group, not against the full baseline sample, which would give a pooled mean of zero [checkable]. The two descriptions can be reconciled only if endline scores were re-standardized against the endline control distribution. In that case the linking step in the pooled model does no work for the effect-size units, and the 0.38 SD is expressed relative to endline-control dispersion [judgment]. This does not change the sign or significance. It does affect the ICCS "38-point" translation (p.11) and cross-study comparisons. The domain subscales are standardized percent-correct scores on unreported numbers of items (p.10), and their baseline controls are the domain percent-correct scores from a partly different baseline item set (Table 3 note, p.11). How those subscales were constructed and matched across waves is not documented [checkable].

*Pre-registration and outcome reporting.* The paper registered the analysis plan in the AEA RCT Registry and says so (fn. 5, p.18), which deserves credit. But the paper gives the registration date without placing it relative to fieldwork. Baseline was "at the beginning of the school year" 2023-24 and endline "near the end of that same school year" (p.8), with no months given [checkable]. I made one WebFetch of the registry page (socialscienceregistry.org/trials/13817), and it succeeded. The page was read through an automated summarizer, so the details below should be confirmed by a reader directly. As retrieved, the registry shows:

- initial registration June 14, 2024; first published June 24, 2024; last updated July 10, 2024;
- intervention dates September 25, 2023 to June 24, 2024;
- primary outcomes "student civic knowledge, student civic attitudes, student civic behaviors," and secondary outcome "teacher pedagogical practices";
- stratification "by county";
- computer-based randomization in the office, with the school as the unit;
- planned observations of 2,100;
- no publicly listed pre-analysis plan document.

Several implications follow.

1. Registration came about nine months after the intervention and baseline began, and within days of the listed intervention end date. It may therefore coincide with or follow endline fieldwork. Calling the study "pre-registered" in the usual sense (before outcome data exist) is not supported [judgment, based on checkable dates].
2. The "planned" 2,100 observations match the realized baseline N of 2,107 (Table 1, p.6), not the design target of 2,800 (p.5). The "ex ante" power calculation uses an average cluster size of 15 (fn. 1, p.18), which equals the realized average (p.8), not the 20 per school the design aimed for (p.5). Both are consistent with the registration and power figures being written after baseline was known [checkable numbers; judgment on inference].
3. Civic attitudes, a registered primary outcome, is relegated to "available upon request" (fn. 3, p.18) and never described in the main text [checkable].
4. The registry says stratification was by county, but the paper says county and district (p.5). The registry says grades 3 and 4 received the intervention, but the paper says grades 1-6 (p.5) [checkable, registry as retrieved]. These are small, but they are the kind of discrepancy a PAP comparison is meant to surface. The paper includes no PAP-deviation discussion [checkable].

*Unreported or untabulated results.* Beyond the attitudes and Teach Primary omissions, several quantitative claims in the text cannot be traced to any exhibit in the PDF [checkable]:

- student textbook use of 63% vs. 2% (p.12);
- baseline engagement levels (p.16);
- the fidelity statistics (96% receipt, 94% take-home, 94% training participation, 38-minute lessons, 29 of 48 respondents reporting two to four monitoring visits; pp.7-8);
- contamination (6 of 70 and 8 of 70 control principals; pp.5-6);
- heterogeneity by teacher covariates, which the text says was estimated (p.10).

Some of these may be in the supplement, which I could not check. As published they rest on trust.

*Verifiability overall.* A reader can check the arithmetic and internal consistency of the reported tables, and it holds. The Ns, follow-up rates, proportion sums in Table 5, the roughly 8-percentage-point upper bound in Table 6 (0.036 + 1.96 × 0.023 ≈ 0.081), and the 15-percentile translation of 0.38 SD all reconcile [checkable]. What a reader cannot check is the step from raw responses to the outcome variables, any specification choice against a genuinely prior plan, or the full set of registered outcomes. Randomization at the school level with 140 clusters and good balance (Table 1, F-test p = .444) makes the core knowledge effect credible on design grounds [judgment]. The reproducibility weaknesses bear most heavily on the secondary claims: subscale and cognitive-domain contrasts, the rural heterogeneity, the classroom-observation mechanisms, and the narrowing of "civic outcomes" in the title to knowledge plus three behavior items. I rate the paper Weak, not Insufficient, because the design and headline model are understandable from the text and the reported numbers cohere. It is not Adequate because the paper provides no data or code pathway, leaves the outcome scaling ambiguous, does not disclose that registration came after baseline, and omits a registered primary outcome. Together these prevent independent verification of the central results [judgment].
